title: Lambda — Serverless Functions
subtitle: Write code, forget servers — event-driven functions that scale to zero and cost nothing when idle

content.text: With EC2, you pay for a server even when it's doing nothing. With Lambda, you pay only when your code runs — and only for the duration it runs (billed in 1ms increments). Lambda scales from 0 to 10,000 concurrent executions automatically, with no configuration. There's no OS to patch, no server to maintain, no auto-scaling groups to configure. You upload code; AWS handles everything else.

content.code:
# Method 1: Direct zip upload
npm run build   # compile TypeScript to JS
zip -r function.zip dist/ node_modules/

aws lambda create-function \
  --function-name my-api \
  --runtime nodejs20.x \
  --handler dist/handler.handler \
  --zip-file fileb://function.zip \
  --role arn:aws:iam::123456789:role/lambda-execution-role

# Update after code changes:
aws lambda update-function-code \
  --function-name my-api \
  --zip-file fileb://function.zip

# Method 2: Container image (for complex dependencies)
# Build and push to ECR, then point Lambda at the image:
aws lambda update-function-code \
  --function-name my-api \
  --image-uri 123456789.dkr.ecr.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/my-app:latest

# Invoke manually for testing
aws lambda invoke \
  --function-name my-api \
  --payload '{"queryStringParameters":{"name":"Alice"}}' \
  response.json
cat response.json

# View logs (Lambda logs go to CloudWatch)
aws logs tail /aws/lambda/my-api --follow

COLD START: The first invocation after a period of inactivity

What happens:
  1. AWS allocates a compute environment (container)
  2. Loads your function code and dependencies
  3. Runs the initialization code (outside handler)
  4. THEN runs your handler

Cold start duration (2026 benchmarks):
  - Node.js 20 with simple handler: 50-200ms
  - Node.js with heavy dependencies (AWS SDK, ORM): 500ms-2s
  - Java / .NET: 2-10s (JVM warmup)
  - Container-based Lambda: 1-5s

Mitigation strategies:
  1. Provisioned concurrency: pre-warm N instances
     → Always warm, no cold starts, higher cost
  2. Minimize package size (tree-shake, remove unused deps)
  3. Move expensive init (DB connections) OUTSIDE the handler:

  // Init outside handler = runs once per container, not per invocation
  const db = new DatabasePool({ ... });  // ← OUTSIDE

  export const handler = async (event) => {
    // db is already connected on warm invocations
    const users = await db.query('SELECT * FROM users');
  };

PRICING (2026):
  Requests: $0.20 per 1M invocations (first 1M/month FREE)
  Duration: $0.0000166667 per GB-second
             (128MB function running 100ms = 0.0128 GB-sec = $0.000000213)

EXAMPLE: API with 10M requests/month, avg 200ms, 256MB memory
  Requests: 10M × $0.20/M = $2.00
  Duration: 10M × 0.2s × 0.256GB × $0.0000166667 = $8.53
  Total: ~$10.53/month

COMPARISON: EC2 t4g.small running 24/7 = $12/month
  → Lambda is cheaper for sporadic traffic
  → EC2 is cheaper for constant high-throughput traffic

  Lambda wins at:
    < 1M requests/month (nearly free)
    Spiky/unpredictable traffic (auto-scales, no idle cost)
    Event-driven workloads (S3, queues, schedules)

  EC2 wins at:
    Constant high-throughput APIs (1000+ req/sec steady state)
    Long-running processes (> 15 minutes — Lambda max timeout)
    Stateful workloads (WebSocket servers, etc.)

questions.question: You initialize a database connection pool inside the Lambda handler function body. What performance problem does this cause?
options: No problem — Lambda handles connection pooling automatically
A new connection pool is created on every invocation, adding 100-500ms latency to each request
Lambda functions cannot connect to databases
The connection pool persists forever causing memory leaks
questions.explanation: Moving initialization code inside the handler means it runs on every invocation — creating a new pool, TCP handshake, TLS negotiation, and auth on every single request. This adds 100-500ms to every invocation. The correct pattern: initialize outside the handler. On a warm Lambda container, the code outside the handler runs once when the container starts. All subsequent invocations on the same container reuse the existing pool — dramatically reducing latency.

faq.q: Can Lambda replace all my backend servers?
faq.a: For many use cases, yes. Lambda is excellent for REST APIs, async processing, scheduled jobs, and event handlers. But Lambda has hard limits: 15-minute max execution time, 10GB max memory, ephemeral filesystem. It's also not ideal for WebSocket servers (connection state), very high throughput (cold starts, pricing), or workloads needing persistent local filesystem access. Lambda + API Gateway covers 80% of web API use cases.

examples: Coca-Cola's vending machines worldwide send events to Lambda functions that process purchases, check inventory, and update analytics — all without any servers managed by their team. The architecture handles millions of transactions daily

Airbnb's image upload pipeline: user uploads a photo → hits API Gateway → Lambda → stores original on S3 → triggers another Lambda (via S3 event) → generates thumbnails → stores on S3 → invalidates CloudFront cache. All in serverless, auto-scaling.
